## About This Project

This project analyzes the 2024 U.S. job market to understand how artificial intelligence is reshaping career opportunities across industries. Using the **Lightcast 2024 dataset** — over 72,000 real job postings — our team applies data science, machine learning, and visualization techniques to explore the divide between AI-driven and traditional careers.

## Research Question

> **How does AI impact job security, salary, and career growth across industries in 2024?**

Specifically, we investigate:

- Which industries are experiencing AI-driven **job growth** vs. **job displacement**?
- How do **salaries** compare between AI and non-AI careers?
- What **skills** differentiate AI roles from traditional ones?
- Are new job titles **emerging** due to AI advancements?

## Research Rationale
Our group shall focus on the research topic “AI vs Non-AI Careers”, given the implementation of AI across industrial sectors remains one of the most relevant forces for either future job growth or displacement. Although AI has existed even before 2020, when it first began its adoption into society at large, only in the past few years and especially since 2024 has the job market been so vividly influenced by its implementation. Jobs have been completely automated and some new ones created, applications to those jobs streamlined under AI overview rather than Human, and industries of all varieties have seen some form of AI implementation, or at least the pressure to adopt it. While other economic factors have contributed to it, the human element behind how AI influences job security, displacement, creation, and otherwise is what our group finds most vital for future analysis.

As such, our group aims to answer how AI impacts job security, which industries are experiencing AI-driven job growth and which job displacement, how do AI-powered careers compare to traditional roles, and are new job titles emerging due to AI advancements alongside these displacements. These aspects reflect the duality of AI, and how universal it has been across industries, rather than limited to a select few and possibly only looking at the negatives. 2024 specifically was reported to have had 23–27% of employees in the U.S. admit to having used AI in their work at least once during the past week, and then about 9–10% claimed they used it every day at work (Bick et al., 2024). Such prevalence of AI, as we hope to find, will tell what the potential future ratio of AI job creation and displacement, and net influences of AI across industries will be. From this, a better grasp of future economic conditions and trends can be found.

## Literature Review
Looking at previous scholarly works, there has already been much research into the impacts of AI across industries in recent years, both positive and negative. To start, based on correlations between AI exposure and stress, anxiety, and burnout within jobs, it was found the implementation of AI to even minor degrees will correlate very strongly with increased job insecurity (Hassan & Anwer, 2024). Instantly, it is clear AI has heavily disrupted current industries and the security which their workers feel, even when not directly threatened with replacement by said AI. The very idea of AI being in the workplace is enough to cause unease, and thus lead to perhaps irrational acts of defense by employees against these models. This isn’t entirely unfounded, however, as more repetitive roles such as communications manager, data entry, mail clerk, and data collector all face the possibility of around 92-98% AI replacement. On the other hand, more complex jobs such as that of a hospitalist, immunologist, physician, and mental health clinician only face around 10% AI replacement, a far cry from the past examples (Balakumar et al., 2024). This displays how while some industries and careers are more prone to AI encroachment, others still remain relatively stable against such displacement. #Data Cleaning & Preprocessing We have removed multiple versions of NAICS and SOC codes because they represent classifications of the same industries and occupations at different levels of detail. For example, NAICS2, NAICS3, NAICS4, NAICS5, and NAICS6 belong to the same industry classification hierarchy, while SOC_2, SOC_3, SOC_4, and SOC_5 belong to the same occupational classification hierarchy. Retaining all levels would result in redundant information and unnecessarily complicate the dataset. Therefore, we will retain one classification level and remove the remaining versions to simplify the dataset, reduce duplication, and improve analytical efficiency. What is worth mentioning, though, is the type of industry, based on metrics such as traditionalism or modernism, is mostly irrelevant to being susceptible to AI encroachment. Even “old school” industries, like farming, see AI implementation in processes like the irrigation of crops, where now models can better analyze the optimal output of water for crops based on certain environmental conditions (Onteddu et al., 2024). So while any industry is capable of being reshaped by AI, the question largely remains whether it will be a net positive or negative. As of now, estimations call for roughly 83 million jobs that are expected to be displaced as a result of AI by 2030, whereas approximately 69 million jobs are to be created for the same reason (Singh, 2025). In terms of this estimate, at least, AI is set to create more displacement than opportunity, yet the full scope of AI’s place in the industry job market is not fully understood, so there is much left to be researched. Overall, though, one cannot deny the impact which AI has had and continues to have on jobs across all economic industries.

## Dataset

| | |
|---|---|
| **Source** | Lightcast 2024 Job Postings |
| **Records** | 72,498 job postings |
| **After cleaning** | 51,316 records |
| **Coverage** | United States, all industries |
| **Key fields** | Salary, ONET codes, skills, education, remote type, industry (NAICS) |

The dataset was cleaned and preprocessed to remove duplicates, impute missing salaries, and standardize classification codes. Full details are in the [Data Preparation](data_cleaning.qmd) section.

## Methodology

1. **Data Cleaning** — Remove redundant classification levels, impute missing salaries, filter outliers
2. **EDA** — Visualize salary distributions, employment trends, and industry patterns
3. **Skill Gap Analysis** — Compare required skills vs. market availability
4. **ML Methods** — KMeans clustering to group job types; Logistic Regression and Random Forest to classify AI vs. non-AI roles
5. **Career Strategy** — Translate findings into actionable career recommendations
